title: Why a Doctor's Visit Costs the Same in Tokyo and in Rural Akita
hook: Why a Doctor's Visit Costs the Same in Tokyo and in Rural Akita
target_query: why do japanese doctor visits cost the same everywhere
free_section_html:
A doctor's visit costs the same in Japan whether it happens at a university hospital in Tokyo or a one-room clinic in rural Akita because the government sets a single national price for almost every medical service, drug, and procedure. This price list is called the shinryo hoshu (診療報酬, "medical treatment remuneration"), and it is revised every two years by Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare after negotiation with a body called the Chuikyo, the Central Social Insurance Medical Council, made up of insurers, doctors' groups, and public representatives.

Every item in the schedule is priced in points, with one point currently worth 10 yen. A basic outpatient consultation, a blood test, an appendectomy, an MRI scan: each has a fixed point value that applies nationwide, regardless of which hospital performs it or how prestigious the surgeon is. A patient covered by any of Japan's public insurance plans pays 30 percent of that fixed price out of pocket, with lower shares for young children and people over 70. The insurer, not the hospital, sets and collects the rest through the public system, so no negotiation ever happens at the reception desk.

This is different from systems where hospitals set their own list prices and insurers negotiate discounts behind the scenes. In Japan, there is nothing to negotiate. A private clinic cannot charge more for the same consultation just because it has nicer furniture, and a public hospital cannot charge less to attract patients. The price is the price, fixed by law under the National Health Insurance Act and the Health Insurance Act, and enforced through the same claims-review system across the country.

What this fixed pricing does not explain, though, is why so many hospitals feel financially squeezed despite a captive national market, why Japanese doctors are famous for seeing dozens of patients in a single morning, and what happens when a patient wants a treatment that isn't on the list at all.
paid_body_html:
The fixed price is only the surface of the system. The deeper story is what a nationally uniform fee schedule does to the incentives of everyone working inside it, and how a country with the price is the price manages, twenty years later, to keep the whole structure from collapsing under an aging population.

How the price list actually gets set

The shinryo hoshu revision is one of the most consequential bureaucratic events in Japanese healthcare, yet it draws little attention outside specialist circles. Roughly every two years, the Chuikyo convenes representatives from the Japan Medical Association, health insurers, employers, and patient advocates to reprice thousands of line items. The overall revision is usually a net reduction, sometimes by a fraction of a percent, sometimes by several percent, because the Ministry of Finance treats each round as an opportunity to slow the growth of national medical spending, which now accounts for a large and rising share of Japan's budget as the population ages.

Individual prices move in both directions. Procedures the ministry wants to encourage, such as home visits for homebound elderly patients or certain forms of dementia care coordination, are sometimes given higher point values to nudge providers toward them. Procedures seen as overused, or drugs whose patents have expired and now face generic competition, tend to be repriced downward. The schedule is, in effect, a five-hundred-page instrument of health policy disguised as a price list.

Why Japanese consultations are so short

Because a clinic cannot raise its prices, and because insurance reimbursement per visit is relatively modest by international standards, providers have historically responded by increasing volume rather than price. This is the origin of what critics, including some Japanese physicians themselves, have called "three-minute medicine": a pattern where general outpatient consultations at busy clinics or hospital outpatient departments move quickly from patient to patient. A clinic paid a fixed sum per consultation earns more by seeing sixty patients in a morning than by spending twenty unhurried minutes with each of twenty.

The same logic pushes providers toward billable add-ons. Because tests, imaging, and injections each carry their own point value, there is a documented tendency for Japanese clinics to order more diagnostic tests per visit than clinics in many other wealthy countries, even when the marginal test adds little diagnostic value. This isn't attributed to individual greed so much as to the mechanical incentive structure: in a system where the base consultation fee is capped, additional billable services are one of the few remaining levers.

What falls outside the price list entirely

Not everything is covered by the shinryo hoshu, and the boundary matters more than most patients realize. Cosmetic surgery, some fertility treatments, certain advanced or experimental therapies, and drugs not yet approved by Japan's regulator sit outside the public schedule and are billed privately, often at prices the provider does set freely. This creates one of the strangest rules in Japanese healthcare: the ban on konsei shinryo (混合診療), or "mixed billing." In most circumstances, a patient cannot combine an insured treatment with an uninsured one in the same course of care and still have the insured portion reimbursed. If a patient wants an unapproved drug alongside standard cancer treatment, for example, the standard treatment can in some cases lose its insurance coverage too, forcing the patient to pay the full cost of everything.

The rule exists to prevent a two-tier system from forming, where wealthier patients pay their way into better-resourced insured care by bundling in extras. Patient advocacy groups and some physicians have pushed for years to loosen it, arguing it blocks access to promising treatments; the Ministry of Health has resisted broad changes, citing the risk of eroding the principle that insured care should not depend on a patient's ability to pay for add-ons. A limited exception, called hyoka ryoyo (evaluation therapy), allows specific advanced or experimental treatments to be combined with insured care in narrow, pre-approved cases, but it remains an exception rather than the rule.

The squeeze nobody sees at the reception desk

The fixed-price structure also explains a pattern outsiders often find puzzling: Japanese hospitals, despite serving a population with universal coverage and heavy healthcare consumption, frequently report thin operating margins, and rural hospitals in particular have been consolidating or closing wards at a steady pace over the past decade. Because no hospital can raise prices to cover rising labor costs, aging infrastructure, or nursing shortages, the biennial downward pressure on point values falls directly onto institutional finances. Larger hospital groups have responded by consolidating smaller facilities, dropping money-losing departments such as maternity wards or emergency overnight care, and concentrating high-reimbursement procedures like advanced cancer surgery in fewer, busier centers.

This is the tension sitting underneath Japan's celebrated universal coverage: the same mechanism that keeps a blood test at a rural clinic the same price as one in Tokyo, and keeps healthcare affordable and equitable on paper, is also the mechanism quietly reshaping which hospitals survive, how long a doctor spends with each patient, and which treatments patients can access only by paying for them entirely on their own.
key_takeaways: Japan prices nearly every medical service through a single national fee schedule, the shinryo hoshu, revised roughly every two years by the health ministry and a negotiating body called the Chuikyo.
Patients pay a fixed 30 percent share of the nationally set price (less for children and people over 70), and no hospital or clinic can legally charge more or less for the same insured procedure.
The fixed pricing pushes providers toward high patient volume and extra billable tests rather than price competition, contributing to Japan's famously short outpatient consultations.

A strict ban on mixing insured and uninsured treatment in one course of care, called konsei shinryo, keeps a two-tier system from forming but also limits patient access to unapproved or experimental treatments.
Because hospitals cannot raise prices to cover rising costs, biennial fee cuts have contributed to the closure or downsizing of money-losing departments, especially in rural hospitals.
